label_provenance.statement: These labels were PROPOSED by an AI agent that read the source code at each finding's line and its callers/config. They are NOT independent human adjudication. Every row has adjudicated=false, independently_adjudicated=false and reviewers=[]. Two distinct human reviewers must confirm or flip each row, set both flags to true and add their own names before the exporter will accept the rows (QR-17).
label_provenance.labelling_convention: expected_route is the cheapest next analysis step given what the scanner's finding shows in place; verdict records my reading of the final truth. So a false positive that can only be ruled out from another file is routed cross_file_analysis, not low_priority. evidence_sufficiency: 2 = the finding's own lines settle it, 1 = needs other files/config/library behaviour, 0 = nothing to go on. needs_human_review is true only for human_review rows.
label_provenance.scope_limits: The shipped Semgrep rules do not parse JSP and spotbugs/dependency-check did not run, so no finding in this project is JSP- or dependency-sourced; jsp_context_analysis therefore has no rows, and dependency_analysis rows are Java findings whose exploitability depends on a library.
label_provenance.rule_id_note: rule_id is the last dotted segment of the Semgrep/gitleaks rule id in the export.

Md5Utils is the primitive behind the password hash md5(loginName + password + salt) in SysPasswordService; plain MD5 for passwords is a real weakness, visible only in the caller.
rows.evidence: Md5Utils.java:22 - algorithm = MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5");; SysPasswordService.java:83 - return Md5Utils.hash(loginName + password + salt);

rows.rationale: MD5 here implements name-based (version 3) UUID generation per the UUID spec, not a security hash.

Session bytes are read from the sys_user_online table and deserialized; they are written by the server (AsyncFactory), so exploitation needs write access to that table, which is a deployment and trust-boundary question.
